question: Lack of EU funding for Cypriot refugees 50 years after the Turkish invasion

This year marks the 50th anniversary of the Turkish invasion and occupation of the northern part of the Republic of Cyprus, with the issue of refugees and displaced persons remaining an open socio-economic wound for Cyprus and Europe.

As in the case of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine – for which continued support worth billions of euro is being provided – it is important to stress that, for its part, Türkiye continues to violate international law and the territorial integrity of the Republic of Cyprus.

The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees estimates that 200 000 Greek Cypriots have been displaced, entailing a violation of the right to housing and to the protection of property as enshrined in the Convention on Human Rights.

Given the prolonged withholding of refugee property and in light of European solidarity between Member States, why have these refugees still not been provided with any compensation through European funds?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.1.2025) The Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) and relevant EU legislation provide for a common policy for third-country nationals requiring international protection in a Member State1, as well as for nationals of a Member State applying for asylum in another Member State2.

The EU asylum legal framework is thus not applicable to the situation described by the Honourable Member. In line with the TFEU, the Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund may support only actions focusing on third-country nationals, including stateless persons or persons with undetermined nationality who are not citizens of the Union3.

A comprehensive settlement of the Cyprus issue would be the quickest and most direct way to solve the problems related to displaced persons and property issues, which have been topics discussed by the leaders of the two Cypriot communities in the framework of negotiations. The matter raised by the Honourable Member once again emphasises the importance of resuming negotiations and reaching a solution.

The EU remains fully committed to a comprehensive settlement of the Cyprus problem within the United Nations (UN) framework, in accordance with all relevant UN Security Council resolutions and in line with the principles on which the EU is founded and the acquis. It is ready to play an active role in supporting all stages of the UN-led process, with all appropriate means at its disposal4.
